<!-- defn-1: body_md -->
\label{defn:scattering_map_flow}
	Given a homoclinic channel $\Gamma$, the scattering map associated to
	$\Gamma$ is a  diffeomorphism from
	$ \textrm{Dom}(\mathcal{S}^\Gamma):=\Omega^\Gamma_-(\Gamma)\subseteq\Lambda$ to
	$ \textrm{Im}(\mathcal{S}^\Gamma):= \Omega^\Gamma_+(\Gamma)\subseteq\Lambda$ given by
	\[\mathcal{S}^\Gamma=\Omega^\Gamma_+\circ (\Omega^\Gamma_-)^{-1}.\]
<!-- end defn-1 -->
<!-- defn-2: body_md -->
\label{defn:transition_map_flow}
	Given a homoclinic channel $\Gamma$ and  (sufficiently large) times $T_-,T_+$, the transition map  $\mathcal{T}=\mathcal{T}^\Gamma_{T_-,T_+}: \Phi_{-T_-}(\textrm{Dom}(\mathcal{S}^\Gamma))\to  \Phi_{T_+}(\textrm{Im}(\mathcal{S}^\Gamma))$ is
	given by
	\begin{equation} \label{eq:SMAndTM}
		\mathcal{T}=\Phi_{T_+}\circ \mathcal{S}^\Gamma\circ\Phi_{T_-}.
	\end{equation}
We write $\mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{x}_-)=\boldsymbol{x}_+$.
<!-- end defn-2 -->
<!-- rem-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:transition_alternative}
In Definition \ref{defn:transition_map_flow} the times $T_+,T_-$ are fixed.
More generally, we can consider $T_+,T_-$ as continuous functions on $\Gamma$. In Section~\ref{sec:transition_map_BNF}, given  a neighborhood  $U$ of the NHIM $\Lambda$, and $\Sigma_+$, $\Sigma_-$ two surfaces of section inside $U$, for any $\boldsymbol{x}\in\Gamma$ we will
define $T_-=T_-(\boldsymbol{x})$ as the first time $t>0$ when  
$\Phi_{-t}(\boldsymbol{x})\in \Sigma_-$, and $T_+=T_+(\boldsymbol{x})$ as the first time $t>0$ when  
$\Phi_{t}(\boldsymbol{x})\in \Sigma_+$.
<!-- end rem-1 -->
<!-- rem-2: body_md -->
In the context of  Sections \ref{sec:BNF} and \ref{sec:transition_map_BNF}, the coordinates $(x,y,\theta)$ represent the normal form coordinates $(x,y,I,\phi)$---with $\theta=(I,\phi)$---as described in \eqref{eq:ReducedSpace}.
<!-- end rem-2 -->
<!-- rem-3: body_md -->
Above, we implicitly assume that
the range of $\tau_i$ intersects the domain of $\tau_{i+1}$, for $i=0,\ldots,N-1$. In the context of the SR3BP, this is automatically satisfied since the scattering map and the corresponding transition maps are globally defined. See Section~\ref{subsec:Series_transition_maps}.
<!-- end rem-3 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:shadowing_topological}
                                                                                                               

Let $\sigma_\alpha$ be a family of scattering maps with associated homoclinic channels $\Gamma_\alpha$, for  $\alpha \in\{1,\ldots, L\}$.

For every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $M_{\min}<M_{\max}$ such that, if 
\[\tau_i= f^{m_i}\circ\sigma_{\alpha(i)}\circ f^{n_i}, i=1,\ldots,N-1,\] 
is a transition map
associated with the homoclinic channel $\Gamma_{\alpha(i)}$, and with $m_i,n_i$ satisfying
 $M_{\min} \le M_i=m_i+n_i \le M_{\max}$,  and if \[\boldsymbol{x}_{i+1}=\tau_i(\boldsymbol{x}_i),  \textrm { for }i=1,\ldots,N-1,\]
then there exists a point $\boldsymbol{y}_1$ whose orbit $\boldsymbol{y}_1,\ldots, \boldsymbol{y}_N$  $\varepsilon$-shadows $\boldsymbol{x}_1,\boldsymbol{x}_2,\ldots, \boldsymbol{x}_N$ in the sense
\begin{equation*}\begin{split}
                                                     
\boldsymbol{y}_{i+1}=&\mathcal{F}^{M_i}(\boldsymbol{y}_i),\textrm { and }\\
d(\boldsymbol{y}_i,\boldsymbol{x}_i)<&\varepsilon\, \textrm{ for } i=1,\ldots,N.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
The orbit $\boldsymbol{y}_1,\ldots, \boldsymbol{y}_N$ is a true orbit of the system. The number of iterates to take $\boldsymbol{y}_i$ to $\boldsymbol{y}_{i+1}$ is $M_i=m_i+n_i$, which is the same as  the number of iterates associated to the transition map  $\tau_i$.

In particular, we can choose the number of iterates $m_i=m_*$, $n_i=n_*$, and $M_i=M_*$ to be independent of $i$.
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- rem-4: body_md -->
We compare Lemma \ref{lem:shadowing_topological} with some similar shadowing lemma type of results. The paper \cite{GideaLlaveSeara20-CPAM} provides a result on shadowing  orbits generated  by scattering maps on a NHIM. The argument requires that the dynamics restricted to the NHIM satisfies Poincar\'e recurrence and, therefore, the shadowing orbits may take a long time. Another result in the paper is on shadowing  orbits obtained by alternately applying scattering maps and iterates of the inner dynamics. While this result does not require Poincar\'e recurrence, it requires that the number of iterates at each step is sufficiently large with respect to the number of iterates at all previous steps. A similar result to the latter appears in \cite{GelfreichT17}.  
Our Lemma~\ref{lem:shadowing_topological}  concerns shadowing orbits of transition maps and gives a uniform number of iterates of the inner dynamics. Since the transition map also encodes the effect of the inner dynamics, and we require that the input of each transition map coincides with the output of the preceding transition map, there is no need to invoke recurrence.
However, this lemma only allows for the shadowing of finite orbits.
<!-- end rem-4 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{th:shadowing}
Let $\left(\boldsymbol{x}_i\right)_{i=1}^N$ be a guiding orbit of the iterated function system (IFS) defined on the reduced NHIM $\Lambda^{\Sigma}_{h}$~\eqref{eq:NHIMred} generated \textbf{solely} by $L\geq 1$ reduced transition maps $\{\mathcal{\tau}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{\tau}_L\}$, expressed in BNF coordinates~\eqref{eq:BNFcoordinates}. 
                                                                                             
Let $\delta$ be the size of the saddle variables~\eqref{eq:ReducedSpace} within the BNF domain $U$,
and assume that the  \emph{homecoming condition}~\eqref{eq:HomecomingCondition} holds.

Then, there exists a true trajectory $\Phi_t({\bf x})$ of the system that $\delta$-shadows the guiding orbit. Specifically, there exists a strictly increasing sequence of times $0 < t_1 < \dots < t_N$ such that
\[
\norm{\Phi_{t_i}({\bf x}) -   \boldsymbol{x}_i } \leq \delta \quad \text{for all } i = 1, \dots, N.
\]
Moreover, if the guiding orbit $\left(\boldsymbol{x}_i\right)_{i=1}^N$ is generated by a sequence of homoclinic segments 
$\left[\boldsymbol{z}_i^-,\boldsymbol{z}_{i+1}^+\right]$, where $\boldsymbol{z}_i^-\in W^\mathrm{u}\left( \boldsymbol{x}_i\right)\cap\Lambda^{\Sigma}_{h}$ and 
$\boldsymbol{z}_{i+1}^+=\Phi_{\boldsymbol{T}^i}\left(\boldsymbol{z}_i^-\right)\in W^\mathrm{s}\left( \boldsymbol{x}_{i+1}\right)\cap\Lambda^{\Sigma}_{h}$, then each $t_i$ can be chosen as $t_i=\boldsymbol{T}^1+\cdots+\boldsymbol{T}^i$, yielding a total drift time of $t_N=\boldsymbol{T}^1+\cdots+\boldsymbol{T}^N$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{th:shadowing_topological}

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
                                                                 
                                    
                                                           

Let $\epsilon_M=\epsilon_M(\delta)$ denote the effect of truncation error~\eqref{eq:errorBNF} of the transformation to BNF variables.

Then, for every $\epsilon>0$ there exist $m_*,n_*$ sufficiently large and a constant $C>0$, such that, for any guiding orbit $\left( \boldsymbol{x}_i\right)_{i=1}^N$ 
given by
\[  \boldsymbol{x}_{i+1}=\tau_i( \boldsymbol{x}_i), \textrm{ for } i=1,\ldots,N-1, \]
where each transition map $\tau_i$ is of the form
\[\tau_i=f^{m_*}\circ\sigma_{\alpha(i)} \circ f^{n_*}, \]
there exists a true trajectory $\Phi_t({\boldsymbol{x}})$ that $(\varepsilon+C\epsilon_M)$-shadows the guiding orbit, 
\[
\norm{\Phi_{t_i}({\boldsymbol{x}}) -   \boldsymbol{x}_i } \leq \epsilon + C \epsilon_M \quad \text{for all } i = 1, \dots, N, 
\]
for some strictly increasing sequence of times $0 < t_1 < \dots < t_N$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- result-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main_numerical}
Consider the SR3BP with a mass ratio given by $\mu_{\text{Sun-Earth}} = 3.040423398444176 \cdot 10^{-6}$, described in Section~\ref{sec:AnalErrorSEBNF}. Let the energy value $c=3.00088$ be fixed.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Following~\cite{DelshamsGR16}, we obtain a semi-analytical approximation of the NHIM $\Lambda_{c}$ around the equilibrium point $L_1$ using the BNF of order $M=16$. 
\item[(b)] Consider a neighborhood $U=U(\delta)$ of size $\delta=0.1$ in the saddle BNF variables. In Section \ref{sec:NumErrorSEBNF} we show that the error of the semi-analytical approximation of the NHIM in $U(\delta)$ is less than $3\times 10^{-7}$. 
\item[(c)]
By part (b), the level sets of $I_\mathrm{v}$ are preserved by the inner map $\mathpzc{f}$ up to an error of $\varepsilon_1=3\times 10^{-7}$. 
                                                                     
In Section~\ref{subsec:Series_transition_maps} we  derive series representations for two different reduced transition maps $\mathcal{\tau}_1, \mathcal{\tau}_2$ that are globally defined on an annulus $\mathcal{A}\subset \Lambda^{\Sigma}_{c}$, corresponding to the range $I_\mathrm{v}\in[I_1,I_2]$, where $I_1=0.001$ and $I_2=0.007$.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 
\item[(d)]
                                                                                                 
In Section~\ref{subsec:Shortest-time_guiding} we find the orbit of the IFS $\{\mathpzc{f},\mathcal{\tau}_1,\mathcal{\tau}_2\}$ that takes the least amount of time to drift from the lower boundary to the upper boundary in $\mathcal{A}$. See Figure~\ref{fig:diffusion-shortest-path-delta-0.1}. It turns out that, in this particular scenario, the shortest-time drift orbit does not use the inner map $\mathpzc{f}$; it consists solely of iterates of the transition maps $\mathcal{\tau}_1, \mathcal{\tau}_2$.
\item[(e)] Let $\left(\boldsymbol{x}_i\right)_{i=1}^{17}$ be the guiding orbit of the IFS $\{\mathcal{\tau}_1, \mathcal{\tau}_2\}$ consisting of the last $N=17$ points in the shortest-time drift orbit found in part (d).
In Section~\ref{sec:Shadowing_trajectory}, we apply the multiple shooting method of Section~\ref{sec:multiple_shooting} to construct a (numerical) shadowing trajectory of the SR3BP close to the guiding orbit. The result is given in Table~\ref{tab:OneCut} and shown in Figure~\ref{fig:shadowing_trajectory}.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end result-1 -->
<!-- rem-5: body_md -->
In the case of the Spatial Restricted 3-Body Problem (SR3BP), for the saddle-center-center equilibrium point considered here, one can take one  the collinear libration points $L_{1,2}$, and compute the BNF around that point.  (For $L_3$, the two center frequencies are close to a  \(1:1\) resonance, so one typically computes  a resonant Birkhoff normal form instead.)
Numerical verifications at the libration point $L_{1}$ of the SR3BP---rather than purely theoretical bounds---show that truncating the normal form to order $M=16$ guarantees an error $\epsilon_M$~\eqref{eq:errorBNF} between the true dynamics and the dynamics induced by the BNF that is less than $3 \times 10^{-7}$ for $\delta=0.1$ and $r=0.05$, at least over short time intervals $t<3$. Further details are provided in Section~\ref{sec:NumErrorSEBNF}, where we illustrate that the analytical bounds for the remainder $R$ are overly pessimistic compared to the numerical estimates for $L_{1}$. This discrepancy is a well-known feature documented by several authors (see, e.g.,~\cite{EfthyGC04,CaraccioloL20}).
<!-- end rem-5 -->
<!-- defn-3: body_md -->
We define the following local Poincaré sections for the flow. The \emph{incoming boundary} is given by 
    $\Sigma_{+}\coloneqq\{\boldsymbol{K}=(x,y,I,\phi)\in \partial U : y=\pm\delta\}$, while the \emph{outgoing boundary} is given by 
    $\Sigma_{-}\coloneqq\{\boldsymbol{K}=(x,y,I,\phi)\in \partial U : x=\pm\delta\}$.
    We also define the section $\Sigma=\{\boldsymbol{K}=(x,y,I,\phi)\in \partial U : \phi_p=0 \}$.
<!-- end defn-3 -->
<!-- defn-4: body_md -->
\label{defn:tplus_tminus}
Let $t_+=t_+\left(s,I,\phi_{\mathrm{p},+}\right)>0$ denote the first time at which the forward trajectory starting at $\boldsymbol{K}_+=(s/\delta,\delta,I,\phi_+)\in\Sigma_{+}$ intersects $\Sigma$ 
at a point $\boldsymbol{k}_+$. This corresponds to the transit time of the primary Poincaré map $\Sigma_{+}\to\Sigma$. 
Analogously, let $-t_-=-t_-\left(s,I,\phi_{\mathrm{p},-}\right)<0$ denote the first time at which the (backward) trajectory starting at $\boldsymbol{K}_-=(\delta,s/\delta,I,\phi_-)\in\Sigma_{-}$ intersects $\Sigma$ at a point $\boldsymbol{k}_-$. This represents the transit time of the primary Poincaré map $\Sigma\to\Sigma_{-}$.
<!-- end defn-4 -->
<!-- rem-6: body_md -->
Although condition~\eqref{eq:OneCut} for a single intersection with $\Sigma\setminus\Sigma_{\pm}$ might seem restrictive, it is easily satisfied in practice. For instance, when $\lambda$ and $\nu_{\mathrm{p}} $ are of the same order of magnitude ($\lambda/\nu_{\mathrm{p}} =O(1)$), we find that $\exp\left(-2\pi\lambda/\nu_{\mathrm{p}} \right)=O(10^{-3})$. Thus, across almost the entire square $\abs{x},\abs{y}\leq \delta$, trajectories inside $U$ cross $\Sigma\setminus\Sigma_{\pm}$ exactly once. Trajectories experiencing multiple intersections are confined to a tiny region extremely close to the invariant axes $x=0$ and $y=0$.
<!-- end rem-6 -->
<!-- rem-7: body_md -->
These type of homoclinic intersections at the ``first cut'' of the asymptotic manifolds with $\mathscr{S}$ are usually called \emph{primary} or \emph{one-round homoclinics}.
<!-- end rem-7 -->
<!-- rem-8: body_md -->
In practice, to determine the homoclinic channels, one can compute all the (primary) homoclinics from $\Lambda$ to $\Lambda$, and then identify continuous families of homoclinics with the property that the restrictions $\Omega_\pm^\Gamma$ are  diffeomorphisms onto their images.
	In~\cite{DGR16}, we illustrate this computation in the case of the SR3BP around the equilibrium point $L_1$, with small enough energy. We show that there are two different homoclinic channels $\Gamma_1, \Gamma_2$. By suitably restricting $\Gamma_1, \Gamma_2$, the associated scattering maps $\mathcal{S}_1, \mathcal{S}_2$ are defined in a common domain.
<!-- end rem-8 -->
<!-- rem-9: body_md -->
$\boldsymbol{Z}_{+}$ ``synchronizes in the far future'' with $\boldsymbol{X}_+$. The wave map $\boldsymbol{Z}_{+} \mapsto \boldsymbol{X}_+$ maps a point to its future synchronized state on the NHIM. The stable manifold $W^{\mathrm{s}}(\boldsymbol{X}_{+})$ is also referred to as the \emph{stable isochrone manifold} of $\boldsymbol{X}_+$.
<!-- end rem-9 -->
<!-- rem-10: body_md -->
In Definition \ref{defn:scattering_map_flow} the scattering map depends only on the choice of the homoclinic channel $\Gamma$, while in Definition~\ref{defn:transition_map_flow} the transition map
additionally depends on the times $T_\pm$, which in turn depend on the sections $\Sigma_{\pm}$.  
	On the one hand, the definition of scattering map is conceptually simpler than the transition map.
	On the other hand, the numerical computation of the transition map is more straightforward. 
	To obtain the scattering map, one would first compute the transition map $\boldsymbol{X}_-\mapsto \boldsymbol{X}_+$, and then derive the scattering map using Equation \eqref{eq:SMAndTM}.
<!-- end rem-10 -->
<!-- rem-11: body_md -->
Note again that in formula~\eqref{eq:SMAndTM} relating the scattering map and the transition map, the flow $\Phi_{T_{\pm}}$ is only needed on the NHIM $\Lambda$ and therefore only involves translations for the angles $\phi=(\phi_\mathrm{p},\phi_\mathrm{v})$ in the BNF variables, that is, the \emph{inner flow} inside the NHIM $\Lambda$ where the actions  $I_\mathrm{s}=0$, $I=(I_\mathrm{p},I_\mathrm{v})$ remain constant.
<!-- end rem-11 -->
<!-- rem-12: body_md -->
\label{rem:time_dependency_tM}
    The reduced transition map depends on the choice of $\Sigma$, a global section within $U$, which in turn uniquely determines  
    the times $t_\pm$. These times must satisfy $\phi_{\mathrm{p}_\pm}\equiv 0\pmod {2\pi}$, so there is an infinite but discrete set of them. However, any two reduced transition maps $\mathcal{\tau}=\mathcal{\tau}(\boldsymbol{T}_\pm)$ and $\mathcal{\tau}'=\mathcal{\tau}'\left(\boldsymbol{T}'_\pm\right)$ are related in the following way
    \[
    \mathcal{\tau} = \Phi_{-\left(\boldsymbol{T}'_+ - \boldsymbol{T}_+\right)} \circ \mathcal{\tau}' \circ \Phi_{-\left(\boldsymbol{T}'_- - \boldsymbol{T}_-\right)}. 
    \]
    If $\mathcal{\tau}$ maps the point $\boldsymbol{x}_-=\left(I_{\mathrm{v},-},\phi_{\mathrm{v},-}\right)$ to $\boldsymbol{x}_+=\left(I_{\mathrm{v},+},\phi_{\mathrm{v},+}\right)$, where, for simplicity of notation, we only write the components $\left(I_{\mathrm{v}},\phi_{\mathrm{v}}\right)$ of $\boldsymbol{x}_\pm$, which are the signicant ones, then $\mathcal{\tau}'$ maps the point
    $\boldsymbol{x}'_-=\left(I'_{\mathrm{v},-},\phi'_{\mathrm{v},-}\right) =\left(I_{\mathrm{v},-},\phi_{\mathrm{v},-} - \left(\boldsymbol{T}'_- - \boldsymbol{T}_-\right)\nu_{\mathrm{v}}\left(I_{\mathrm{v},-}\right)\right)$ to
    $\boldsymbol{x}'_+=\left(I'_{\mathrm{v},+},\phi'_{\mathrm{v},+}\right) =\left(I_{\mathrm{v},+},\phi_{\mathrm{v},+} + \left(\boldsymbol{T}'_+ - \boldsymbol{T}_+\right)\nu_{\mathrm{v}}\left(I_{\mathrm{v},+}\right)\right)$.
   Thus, both pre-images $\boldsymbol{x}_-$ and $\boldsymbol{x}'_-$ have the same action $I_{\mathrm{v},-}$ but their angle differs by a shift.
    Similarly, both images $\boldsymbol{x}_+$ and $\boldsymbol{x}'_+$ have the same action $I_{\mathrm{v},+}$ but their angle differs by a shift.
<!-- end rem-12 -->
<!-- defn-5: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{\tau}_1, \mathcal{\tau}_2, \dotsc, \mathcal{\tau}_{L}$ be reduced transition maps defined on $\Lambda^{\Sigma}_{h}$.
Any finite orbit of the IFS $\{f,\mathcal{\tau}_1,\ldots, \mathcal{\tau}_L\}$ consisting of the inner map and transition maps will be referred to as a \emph{guiding orbit}.
<!-- end defn-5 -->
<!-- rem-13: body_md -->
\label{rem:Zpm_to_tZpm}
$\boldsymbol{Z}_\pm$ and $\boldsymbol{z}_\pm$ are simply related by the flow: $\boldsymbol{z}_\pm = \Phi_{\pm t_\pm}(\boldsymbol{Z}_\pm)$.
<!-- end rem-13 -->
<!-- defn-6: body_md -->
The sequence of pairs $(\boldsymbol{Z}^-_i, \boldsymbol{Z}^+_{i+1})_{i=1}^{N-1}$ will be called a \emph{pseudo-trajectory} of the system, while the sequence of pairs $(\boldsymbol{z}^-_i, \boldsymbol{z}^+_{i+1})_{i=1}^{N-1}$ will be called a \emph{reduced pseudo-trajectory}.
<!-- end defn-6 -->
<!-- rem-14: body_md -->
\label{rem:reduced_pseudo_orbit}
The sequence of points $(\boldsymbol{z}^-_i)_{i=1}^{N-1}$ determines a finite \emph{pseudo-orbit} in the classical sense of dynamical systems~\cite{Bowen75,KPC07}: there is an associated sequence $(h_i)_{i=1}^{N-2}$ of positive times, $h_i = T_{\mathrm{ext}}^i+t_-^i+t_+^{i+1}$, such that
\[ \norm{\boldsymbol{z}^-_{i+1} - \Phi^{h_i}(\boldsymbol{z}^-_i)} \leq \delta \quad \text{for }i=1,\dotsc,N-2,\]
where we are using the maximum norm.
Notice that 
$\Phi^{h_i}(\boldsymbol{z}^-_i) = \boldsymbol{z}^+_{i+1}$. Indeed, for all $i$, both points $\boldsymbol{z}^-_i$ and $\boldsymbol{z}^+_i$ are $\delta$-close to $\boldsymbol{x}_i$:
\begin{align*}
    \norm{\boldsymbol{z}^+_i - \boldsymbol{x}_i} = \abs{y} &= \rho_+:=\,\mathrm{e}^{-t_+\,\lambda}\delta\leq \delta, \\
    \norm{\boldsymbol{z}^+_i - \boldsymbol{x}_i} = \abs{x} &= \rho_-:= \,\mathrm{e}^{ -t_-\,\lambda}\delta\leq \delta.
\end{align*}
In our particular scenario, pseudo-orbits specifically consist of points on homoclinic orbits to $\Lambda^{\Sigma}_{h}$, not general orbits.
See Figure~\ref{fig:pseudo_orbit}.
<!-- end rem-14 -->
<!-- defn-7: body_md -->
A \emph{shadowing trajectory} is a trajectory of the system that passes close to the pseudo-trajectory, i.e., close to all the points $(\boldsymbol{Z}^-_i, \boldsymbol{Z}^+_{i+1})_{i=1}^{N-1}$.
<!-- end defn-7 -->
<!-- rem-15: body_md -->
Condition~\eqref{eq:HomecomingCondition} is sufficient but not necessary to guarantee that the sequence of points $\boldsymbol{K}_i^\pm$ remains within $U$ with trajectories intersecting $\Sigma$ exactly once. For example, in Section~\ref{sec:semianalytical_results} we obtain a numerical trajectory of the SR3BP system that $\delta$-shadows the guiding orbit, whose points $\boldsymbol{K}_i^\pm$ remain within $U$ with trajectories intersecting $\Sigma$ exactly once, even though~\eqref{eq:HomecomingCondition} is not satisfied. See Remark~\ref{rem:shadowing_thm}.
<!-- end rem-15 -->
<!-- rem-16: body_md -->
Figure~\ref{fig:shadowing} only shows a projection of the trajectories onto the saddle variables $x,y$. In fact, the action and angle variables $I,\phi$ must also match at the points $(\boldsymbol{K}^-_i, \boldsymbol{K}^+_{i+1})_{i=1}^{N-1}$.
<!-- end rem-16 -->
<!-- rem-17: body_md -->
Since $s_i=\delta^i_-\delta^i_+\neq 0$, the time $t_\pm^i=t_\pm^i(s_i,I^i)$ and frequency $\nu=\nu(s_i,I^i)$ used here is different from the time  $t_\pm^i=t_\pm^i(0,I^i)$ and frequency $\nu=\nu(0,I^i)$ used for $s=0$ in \eqref{eq:Zi}: $t_\pm^i(s_i,I^i)=(1+O(s_i))t_\pm^i(0,I^i)$, so $\boldsymbol{K}^-_i$ and $\boldsymbol{Z}^-_i$ differ not only in coordinate $y$, but also slightly in $\phi$.
<!-- end rem-17 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:bounds}
   Let $a=20$ and $b=548\cdot 3$. Let $H(X, Y)=\sum_{s \geqslant 2} H_{s}(X, Y)$ with $H_{2}$ given in~\eqref{eq:H2} and $\left\|H_{s}\right\| \leq c^{s-2}d$  for $s \geq 2$. Assume that the lower bounds for the resonances $\alpha_s$ given in~\eqref{eq:alphas} satisfy $\alpha_s>0$ for $2\leq s \leq M$.  Then
   
\noindent a) $\displaystyle \left\|\mathcal{Z}_{s}\right\|\leq\frac{\frac{1}{6}(6cd)^{s-2}(s-2)!}{\alpha_{3} \cdots \alpha_{s-1}}$
for $s$ even, $4\leq  s \leq M$,

\noindent b) $\displaystyle \left\|\mathcal{R}_{s}^{(M)}\right\|\leq\frac{a d^2(a c d)^{s-2}(M-3)!(M-2)^{s-M+2}}{\,\alpha_{3} \cdots \alpha_{M-1} \alpha_{M}^{s-M+2}}$ for $s\geq M+1$,

\noindent c) Defining $\displaystyle r_{M}^{*}=\frac{\alpha_{M}}{b c d M}$,
$\Psi^{(M)}$ is analytic on $\hat{\mathcal{B}}_{r_{R}^{*}}$ and, for any $r \leq r_{R}^{*}$, one has the inclusion
$\Psi^{(M)}\left(\mathcal{B}_{r}\right)\supset \mathcal{B}_{r / 2}$.
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
One can use Stirling's formula
$\displaystyle n!=\sqrt{2 \pi n}\left(\frac{n}{e}\right)^{n}\left(1+O\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\right)$
 to get 
 \[
 \frac{(M-3)!}{(M-2)^{M-2}}=\frac{(M-3)}{\mathrm{e}^{M-2}}\left(1+O\left(\frac{1}{M-2}\right)\right).
 \]
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
$\displaystyle\frac{\alpha_{M}^{M-2}}{\alpha_{3} \cdots \alpha_{M-1}}=
\frac{\alpha_{M}}{\alpha_{3}} \cdots \frac{\alpha_{M}}{\alpha_{M-1}}\leq 1$.
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- rem-18: body_md -->
The orbit error of $\boldsymbol{Z}$ is calculated over a time span of $T=3$ units because this is the approximate period of vertical and horizontal oscillations of solutions around the equilibrium point.
<!-- end rem-18 -->
<!-- rem-19: body_md -->
The scattering map cannot be used to design optimal time guiding orbits. It is defined through asymptotic homoclinics, so it does not carry any information on time. In this situation, it is necessary to use the transition map.
<!-- end rem-19 -->
<!-- rem-20: body_md -->
\label{rem:shadowing_thm}
Theorem~\ref{th:shadowing} does not apply in this situation. This particular guiding orbit has $N=17$. All other variables ($\chi, \lambda, \nu_{\mathrm{p}}$) depend on the homoclinic point $\mathcal{K}^{i}$, so they vary slightly for each homoclinic segment. However, in practice, we find that these variables do not change much across homoclinics, and remain very close to the following values: $\chi \approx 2.79$, $\lambda \approx \lambda^0 = 2.53$, $\nu_{\mathrm{p}} \approx \nu_{\mathrm{p}} ^0 = 2.08$. Thus, the homecoming condition~\eqref{eq:HomecomingCondition} is not satisfied,
\[ (N-1)\chi \approx 44.64 \nless \pi\lambda/\nu_{\mathrm{p}} \approx 3.82. \]
